summary: Specifies how to use SCTP as a transport between SIP entities. SCTP offers features that may help SIP entities that exchange many messages, such as gateways and proxies. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP phone messages can travel in different kinds of trucks. This memo says how to use a special truck, SCTP, that handles lots of packages without getting stuck behind one slow one.

subtitle: How SIP messages ride on SCTP, and why that can help busy proxies and gateways.

tldr.problem: SIP is transport-independent, but its procedures were defined only for UDP and TCP, even though SCTP has features that suit entities exchanging many messages.
tldr.mechanism: SIP over SCTP works almost like SIP over TCP. A sender SHOULD put each message on stream zero with the unordered flag set, unless TLS or another ordered layer is in use. The RFC also defines the Via value TLS-SCTP and the NAPTR service SIPS+D2S.
tldr.outcome: SIP entities get a third transport option whose benefits mostly appear when packets are lost. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4168 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP, RFC 2960) is a transport protocol at the same layer as TCP and UDP. It was designed with the transport of legacy SS7 signaling messages in mind. The authors observed that many of its features also help carry SIP, the Session Initiation Protocol (RFC 3261).

SIP can run over any reliable or unreliable message or stream transport, but procedures were only defined for UDP and TCP. RFC 4168 defines transport of SIP over SCTP. The abstract notes that support is a relatively straightforward process, nearly identical to support for TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: SCTP was built for carrying phone-system signals, and it turns out to be good for carrying SIP messages too. This memo explains how.

sections.title: Potential Benefits
sections.content:
Against UDP, SCTP shares the advantages of any connection-oriented transport. Fast retransmit lets SCTP notice a lost packet quickly, whereas detection over UDP takes at least 500 ms. The RFC calls this probably the most significant advantage for SIP. Congestion control covers the whole association, so the aggregate message rate between two entities can be controlled, instead of per transaction as with SIP over UDP. Transport-layer fragmentation avoids IP fragmentation, which raises the chance of loss and makes NAT and firewall traversal difficult.

Against TCP, the main gain is avoiding head-of-line blocking. SCTP is message-based and can deliver messages as soon as they arrive when using its unordered service, so a lost message in one SIP transaction does not hold up another. Message boundaries also make parsing easier, though the RFC calls that advantage almost negligible. Multihoming lets one association use several IP addresses, but because SIP can already fail over with SRV records, the RFC calls its benefit marginal.

Most benefits appear under loss. With zero loss, SCTP should perform on par with TCP, and the RFC says research is needed to learn at which loss levels improvements show.
sections.plainLanguage: SCTP notices lost packages sooner than UDP does, and a stuck package does not block the ones behind it, as it would with TCP. You mostly notice this when things go wrong.

sections.title: The TLS-SCTP Transport Parameter
sections.content:
The Via header field carries a transport identifier. RFC 3261 defines SCTP but no value for TLS over SCTP, and its TLS value is meant for TLS over TCP. RFC 4168 therefore adds TLS-SCTP for requests sent over TLS over SCTP.

The updated grammar is transport = "UDP" / "TCP" / "TLS" / "SCTP" / "TLS-SCTP" / other-transport.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message carries a label saying which kind of truck it rode in. This memo adds a label for the truck that is both locked (TLS) and SCTP.

sections.title: Sending SIP Over SCTP
sections.content:
Rules for sending a request are identical to TCP, except that an SCTP sender must pick a stream within the association. No SCTP identifier is needed for SIP, so the Payload Protocol Identifier in DATA chunks carrying SIP messages MUST be set to zero. The SIP transport layers of both peers manage the persistent SCTP connection between them.

To avoid head-of-line blocking, a SIP entity SHOULD send every message, request or response, over stream zero with the unordered flag set. A receiver MUST be ready to receive SIP messages on any stream. Using stream IDs as lightweight transaction identifiers was proposed earlier but withdrawn, since the branch parameter of Via entries now identifies transactions.

TLS over SCTP, as defined in RFC 3436, MUST NOT use unordered delivery, and neither may any other layer that needs ordered delivery. In that case, messages of the same SIP transaction SHOULD go on the same stream, and different transactions SHOULD use different streams while enough streams are available. Each side manages its own sending streams, so a response may come back on a different stream than the request.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally every message goes in the same lane but without a fixed order, so none waits on another. If a locked (TLS) lane is used, order matters, so each conversation gets its own lane.

sections.title: Locating a SIP Server
sections.content: The main question before sending is whether the next hop supports SCTP. SIP entities use the normal discovery procedures from RFC 3263. For TLS over SCTP an extra definition is needed. RFC 3263 defines the NAPTR service value SIP+D2S for SCTP but none for TLS over SCTP, so RFC 4168 defines SIPS+D2S for servers that support TLS over SCTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending, you look up in a directory whether the other side can receive by SCTP. This memo adds a directory entry for the locked version.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security issues in RFC 3261 are not worsened by SCTP, provided the advice in Section 5.1 is followed and TLS over SCTP is used wherever TLS would be required by RFC 3261 or RFC 3263. The mechanisms in RFC 3436 MUST be used when SIP runs over TLS and SCTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Using SCTP does not make SIP less safe if you follow the rules and use the locked version when it is needed.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC defines one new NAPTR service field value, SIPS+D2S. IANA registered it in the registry for the SIP SRV Resource Record Services Field, with protocol SCTP and reference RFC 4168.
sections.plainLanguage: The new directory label was written into the official list of labels.
